prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the discovery in this list that I find hardest to argue against. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes light shifts by design, and the realisation, above all in strontium at JILA and RIKEN, has brought fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level. This is nature answering back. Clocks in different laboratories agree, they resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetres, they constrain drifts of constants and they put limits on ultralight dark matter. It is also the one candidate with seven of eight members ranking it, three of them first, and a clean two-person attribution that no colleague has contested. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize recognised neighbouring steps but not the neutral-atom lattice clock itself, so a citation can be written without overlap. As Secretary I would also note that the redefinition of the second is a very concrete measure of maturity.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that a clock is an instrument, and the committee has to ask whether this is a discovery or an engineering triumph. I would answer that the 'discovery' is the demonstrated ability to cancel systematic shifts for thousands of atoms at once, and what that opens in physics, but I accept that a colleague could reasonably weigh it as precision metrology. A second concern is credit. The ion-clock community and contributors such as Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley can be argued for, and I am relying on my recollection of the history, not on checked documents. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so some of the impact is still prospective.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and proposes MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, stressing the unusually direct loop between theory and experiment and the independent confirmation across moire platforms.
responses.response: I agree that the theory-experiment loop is the most appealing feature of B001, and it is why I keep it second, and it is my first alternative. I part company with Olle on two points. First, the superconducting pairing and several correlated states are still disputed, and I am wary of crowning a field whose central phenomenon has no settled mechanism, especially when the strongest confirmation is that many groups see the same phase diagram, not that the theory explains it. Second, I would drop Bistritzer, but I concede that dropping him is awkward given the 2011 prediction, and the three-name version is the more faithful attribution. A two-name prize would give Bistritzer's decisive calculation too little credit, so I am unsure whether my own two-name version is defensible, and I would like Olle to say who he would remove if only two were possible.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first, arguing that it is a clean case of foundational quantum optics becoming the enabling platform of superconducting processors, and a natural follow-on to the 2025 circuit prize; he also ranks the clocks second.
responses.response: I respect Goran's expertise here, and circuit QED is certainly an important step. But I read the 2025 prize as having already covered the macroscopic quantum behaviour of superconducting circuits, and the committee should be careful about awarding the same platform again so soon. The claim that cQED is the foundation of all processors is also a statement about technology and engineering, while the clocks have already produced new tests of physics. B058 also has a credit problem he himself notes: Wallraff made the decisive first strong-coupling experiment and is outside the named three. I do not see that gap closing, so for now I keep it out of my configuration. I am glad that Goran ranks the clocks second, because that shows B007 is robust to the choice of first place.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first, as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, with Halzen and Karle as the central names; he places the clocks second.
responses.response: Mark's argument is the one closest to my own criterion, since a purpose-built detector that opens a new window is precisely discovery-first physics, and I ranked B039 third for that reason. My hesitation is maturity and attribution. The diffuse flux is confirmed within IceCube channels, but independent confirmation of source associations from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD is still thin, and the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results are recent. With a collaboration of this size the choice between Halzen, Karle and Spiering is also a matter of judgement, not of documents. I would keep B039 as a serious alternative and would be prepared to move it up if the expert reports we commission show that the source associations hold up.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clocks first on the grounds that they are a new measurement capability at the 1e-18 level that opens other science, and notes that the credit between Katori and Ye is clean while ion-clock and comb work were recognised elsewhere.
responses.response: I am grateful for Stefan's support and for his judgement from the experimentalist side that the systematic-control work behind the 1e-18 figure is the real achievement. I would add one qualification to our shared view. The strongest version of our case is not that the clocks are accurate but that this accuracy has produced physics, and the citation should say so. I would be cautious about wording that makes it sound like a purely technological award. On his second choice, atom interferometry, I see merit, but the missing Chu and the split between Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich make the attribution much less clean than for the clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee as a whole will treat optical lattice clocks as a physics discovery rather than as metrology, and how the citation should be worded to reflect that.
Whether the expert reports would add other names (for example Lemonde, Ludlow or Hinkley, or ion-clock pioneers) that would force a more careful allocation than Katori and Ye.

Whether the committee prefers a second part, such as moire quantum matter, in the same year, which would need three or fewer names across both parts and so a hard choice among MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer.
How mature the IceCube source associations are, until independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD is available.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B007 or the other shortlisted candidates; my own research (string theory, quantum gravity, cosmology) and my links to Gross, Rubinstein and Van Riet do not touch any shortlisted candidate. As Secretary I have a procedural role in commissioning expert reports, which is not a personal connection to any candidate.
